headline: Medium prompt-injection and cascading-error risk from shared-bus Pipecat outputs into a non-runnable knowledge list; no direct data-leak path is evidenced.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is non-runnable and has no I/O surfaces, so it cannot ingest Pipecat output by itself. But pipecat supports stdin/stdout and shared-bus session scope, so if an operator bridges its text into the list workflow, prompt-like content could be copied into downstream handling. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF an operator copies Pipecat text into the awesome-selfhosted curation workflow
IF Pipecat output is treated as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Use a manual review step before pasting any Pipecat output
Strip imperative language from imported text
Keep Pipecat and curation tasks in separate sessions
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to imported snippets

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-selfhosted touches no data classes and has no network egress, so it is not a meaningful leak source. Pipecat touches text, audio, video, images, and conversation state and can egress to allowlisted APIs, but the pair lacks a shared workspace or authenticated data bridge in the profiles. Leakage is therefore only plausible through unusual operator handling.
conditions: IF sensitive text from Pipecat is manually copied into the awesome-selfhosted repository or issue tracker
IF Pipecat is configured to send conversation content to an external allowlisted API
mitigations: Avoid pasting conversation content into the list repo
Keep Pipecat API keys scoped to the minimum needed
Review allowlisted endpoints before enabling them

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is not runnable and exposes no write surfaces, while pipecat is a framework with shared-bus session scope but no filesystem or git write capability is documented. With no overlapping mutable resource in the profiles, a write-write conflict pathway is not evidenced.
conditions: IF a separate orchestrator grants both agents write access to the same mutable resource
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces
Do not mount a shared writable directory
requires-engineering: add explicit locking around any shared resource

D_cascading_error.rationale: Pipecat can emit conversational text over stdin/stdout and shared bus, while awesome-selfhosted is a knowledge-management list that could be updated from that text by an operator. If Pipecat output is treated as authoritative curation input, errors can cascade into incorrect listings or metadata. The pairwise pathway is inferred from profiles, not directly observed.
conditions: IF Pipecat-generated text is used as the source for list edits
IF no human verification occurs before publishing changes
mitigations: Require human verification of every imported fact
Compare Pipecat output against primary sources
Use a checklist for publication-ready entries

E_compliance.rationale: No PHI, residency, or retention obligations are documented for awesome-selfhosted, and pipecat only shows generic data classes plus allowlisted egress. Because the profiles do not specify regulated data handling or mismatched jurisdictions, only a limited compliance concern is supportable. The other agent is not cited beyond its lack of regulated-data indicators.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is routed through Pipecat
IF the operator publishes that data into the awesome-selfhosted project artifacts
mitigations: Do not route regulated data through the pair
Review retention settings on any Pipecat backend
Avoid storing personal data in list entries
